blocks.alt: Electrician Van Wrap in Toronto CNR Electric's Ford Transit Partial Wrap

blocks.html:
Electrician van wrap projects live or die on one question: can a homeowner read your phone number and licence number before the light turns green? CNR Electric brought us a red Ford Transit wanting exactly that — a high-contrast Ford Transit partial wrap that turned a plain cargo van into a sales tool without repainting a panel. Here is what we installed in Etobicoke, why partial coverage was right, and the Ontario compliance rule most contractors in the GTA get wrong.

What We Installed on CNR Electric’s Ford Transit

The van arrived in factory red with a ladder rack mounted, which shaped the layout: rack hardware eats into the upper panels where most shops put a logo. Our design team worked around it:

  • Rear door glass: “CNR Electric LTD”, phone number and the Industrial – Commercial – Residential line, sized to read from two car lengths back
  • Side glass: a printed panel listing service upgrades, EV chargers, lighting and renovations
  • Hood graphic: a compact mark that identifies the van head-on in a driveway
  • Reflective striping: front and rear, for unlit residential streets on evening calls

Because the panels stayed factory red, the job used a fraction of the film a full wrap needs. The glass did the heavy lifting.

Why a Ford Transit Partial Wrap Beats a Full Wrap Here

When the factory paint is already a strong brand colour — CNR’s red is a good example — a partial wrap borrows that colour for free and spends the budget on information only.

For CNR Electric, a Ford Transit partial wrap delivered near-full-wrap legibility at lower cost, with less downtime.

The Ontario Rule Most Electricians Miss

In Ontario, a Licensed Electrical Contractor must display their ECRA/ESA licence number on business vehicles, and the Electrical Safety Authority is specific about how. Per the ESA’s requirements to display your licence, it must be at least one inch (2.54 cm) high, in black or white lettering, on the back or both sides, prefixed with “ECRA/ESA Lic” or “ECRA/ESA” — within 90 days of the licence date. The ECRA/ESA logo cannot be used if the company name does not appear on the vehicle, and never on its own.

We raise this on every electrician van wrap we quote. A design that buries a 3/4-inch licence number in a dark corner has to be redone.

This is general information, not legal advice — confirm your current obligations directly with the ESA.

Glass Graphics and the Rear-View Rule

Graphics on van glass are normal practice, but Ontario’s Highway Traffic Act sets limits. Section 74 requires a clear view through the windshield and front side windows. For the rear window it provides an exemption where mirrors give the driver a clearly reflected view behind — which covers most cargo vans, including this Transit. So we never apply opaque graphics to the windshield or front side windows, we use perforated one-way vision film for full glass coverage, and we confirm the mirrors are adequate first.

Material and Cost Factors in the GTA

Cargo van panels are not flat. Between rivets, seams and corrugated sections, a partial wrap needs cast film — 3M’s Controltac IJ180Cv3 is specified for fleet graphics including corrugations and rivets. Calendered film costs less up front, then shrinks out of those recesses within a couple of Canadian winters.

Typical GTA range for a commercial van partial wrap: roughly $1,800–$3,800 CAD. Glass-only decal packages sit well below that. These are general market estimates, not a quote — every van is priced from its own measurements.

Mistakes We See on Contractor Vans

  • Too much copy. Nine service items read as a grey block at 60 km/h. CNR’s van lists four.
  • Low-contrast lettering. Dark type on a dark panel disappears at dusk, when many service calls happen.
  • No licence number in the design brief. It gets added later, badly.
  • Skipping the overlaminate. Road salt and pressure washing ruin unprotected print.
  • Wrapping over rust. Vinyl hides corrosion while it spreads. The same discipline applies across contractor and trades fleets.

FAQ: Electrician Van Wrap in Toronto

  1. How much does an electrician van wrap cost in Toronto?

    A partial wrap on a cargo van typically runs about $1,800–$3,800 CAD in the GTA, depending on coverage, design and film choice. Lettering and decal packages cost considerably less.

  2. How long does a Ford Transit partial wrap take to install?

    Most partial wraps install in one to two days once the design is approved and the van is clean. Design and proofing take a few business days before that.

  3. Do I have to put my ECRA/ESA licence number on my van?

    Yes. Ontario requires Licensed Electrical Contractors to display it on business vehicles within 90 days of the licence date — at least one inch high, in black or white lettering, on the back or both sides.

  4. Can I put graphics on my van’s rear window in Ontario?

    Generally yes for cargo vans. The Highway Traffic Act exempts the rear window where mirrors give a clear reflected view behind. Windshields and front side windows must stay unobstructed.

  5. How long will an electrician van wrap last in Canada?

    Professionally installed cast vinyl with an overlaminate commonly performs five to seven years on vertical panels; hoods and roofs weather faster from UV. We include a three-year warranty against peeling, bubbling and fading.

Ready to Brand Your Electrical Fleet?

A well-built electrician van wrap works every hour that van sits in a driveway, and it costs less per impression than almost any other advertising a contractor in Etobicoke, Toronto, Mississauga, Brampton or Vaughan can buy. Whether it is one Ford Transit or eight vans needing consistent branding across Ontario, our design team and certified installers handle the job.

Call us at 416-746-1381, email info@VinylWrapToronto.com, or visit 24 Ronson Dr, Unit 1, Etobicoke, ON. Free estimates, fast turnaround, and a three-year warranty on every wrap we install.
